newsitem.title: UK: UK backs body to defuse N.Irish parade conflicts.
newsitem.headline: UK backs body to defuse N.Irish parade conflicts.

text.p: The British government agreed on Thursday to create a commission to try to defuse sectarian tension sparked by the annual parade season in Northern Ireland.

But Northern Ireland Minister Patrick Mayhew said it needed more time to decide whether the commission, as recommended by an independent review body, should have legal powers to decide whether disputed parades by the Protestant majority go ahead.
Mayhew immediately came under fire from the opposition for failing to act immediately to give the commission legal powers.

Labour member of parliament Kevin McNamara accused Mayhew of "dodging the issue". An election is due by May 22 and the Conservative government relies on the support of Protestant politicians from Northern Ireland to guarantee its survival in parliament where it has as many MPs as the combined opposition.

Thursday's announcement follows the publication of a report commissioned by the government from a three-man team, headed by leading academic Peter North, on how to deal with controversial parades and prevent them setting off sectarian clashes.
The report said a five-member "parades commission", rather than the police, should act as mediators and eventually decide whether marches near Catholic areas should go ahead.

But the largely Protestant police force would have the right of appeal if they believed public order was endangered. It also called for a code of conduct for parades and for anyone who breached a ruling of the commission to be penalised.
Two people were killed and many injured during a summer frenzy of sectarian violence last year which began with a march in the town of Drumcree, 30 miles (40 km) south of Belfast.
This was followed by arson attacks on churches and boycotts of Catholic and Protestant traders in some rural communities.
Thursday's publication of the report coincided with the 25th anniversary of Bloody Sunday when 13 Catholics on a civil rights march were shot dead by British troops in Londonderry.
Nationalist Northern Irish politicians are worried that if the government does not act fast, the marching season -- which begins in the late spring -- could already be underway.

Northern Ireland has been hit by a series of bombings in recent weeks by the Irish Republican Army, which seeks a united Ireland and scrapped a September 1994 ceasefire in February. Protestant guerrillas are still holding to their truce.
Mayhew said he expected consultation to be over by March but critics believe any legislation could be lost if an election is called earlier.

"To delay consultation until the period just before the general election is called...can only encourage the (Protestant) Unionists to believe that they can, as a price for their support of the government, require this power to be withdrawn," minority Liberal Democrat leader, Paddy Ashdown, told parliament.
The Unionists back continued British rule in the province.

Mo Mowlam, the opposition Labour party's Northern Ireland spokeswoman, urged the government to act immediately on the "guts of the report". Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring also called for the report to be given the go-ahead at once.
"Whatever reservations there may be on points of detail, it is vital in view of the imminence of the marching season that its key recommendations should be implemented without delay," he said.
Last year's violence dealt a body blow to efforts to bring peace to the province after more than 25 years of strife.
Protestants deny Catholic charges of bigotry and say their marches show their loyalty to their faith and the British Crown.
But Catholics regard them as triumphalist commemorations of 300-year-old victories over the native Irish.
